The reason we've never really pursued big energy products is because energy, to date, has always been a major constraint. Imagine what we could do by bumping our energy production up a couple of magnitudes. That's possible with renewables. That's not possible with things like nuclear unless you want to start getting hundreds to thousands of nuclear plants in each and every single state. And at that scale nuclear catastrophes would become a regular part of life. We can work to minimize this risk, but these are highly complex systems and things will go wrong.

There's also the fact that nuclear is not renewable. Uranium is consumed. Breeder reactors could mitigate this in exchange with produces vast quantities of weapons grade plutonium. As we head into the twilight of fossil fuels, I think it's important we actually think about the future this time around. We want energy with scalability, safety, practically infinite supply (including at potentially exponential usage levels), and decentralization would also be a perk. The decentralization is great not only for people but for the energy itself. Imagine a state is dependent on a nuclear reactor and the nuke has a meltdown. If the state were genuinely dependent on that reactor, the nuclear meltdown would cause a dual crisis. Something similar happened recently in California when a natural gas pipeline sprung a leak. Thanks to the extreme centralization of power that pipeline leak translated to blackouts for hundreds of thousands of Californians. Centralization without multiple redundancies means you'll never truly robust energy.
